analysis.one_liner: Restores the right to sue nuclear weapons contractors directly for radiation injuries from testing.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in May 1989, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1985, Congress passed a law that replaced the people being sued in radiation-injury lawsuits — instead of suing the private contractors who ran atomic weapons testing programs, injured people had to sue the federal government, and that became their only legal remedy. This bill would repeal that law, letting victims sue the contractors directly again. It would also pause the legal filing deadlines so that people whose earlier lawsuits were thrown out, or whose time ran out while the 1985 law was in effect, could get a new chance to file.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured, made sick, or killed by radiation from atomic weapons testing programs — downwind residents, test-site workers, and their families — who under the 1985 law could only sue the federal government instead of the private companies that actually ran the test sites. The bill would also reopen the door for people whose earlier lawsuits were dismissed under the 1985 law, by pausing the filing deadlines for their cases.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 1985 provision that substituted the United States as the defendant in suits against private contractors for radiation injuries from atomic weapons testing, and that made the Federal Tort Claims Act the sole remedy for those injuries [S2][S3].

Pauses the clock on federal and state filing deadlines for the period the 1985 law was in effect, and lets people whose pre-1985 lawsuits were dismissed under it restart the clock from their original filing [S3].
Gives claims whose filing deadline would expire within a year of enactment a one-year window to be filed before being barred forever [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The private contractors that ran atomic weapons testing programs, who would again face direct lawsuits and potential jury verdicts for radiation injuries; any added litigation and settlement costs in the weapons complex could ultimately flow into defense program costs borne by taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 1985 shield exposes weapons-testing contractors to direct liability and potentially large verdicts; the 1985 provision channeled claims to the government under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which caps damages and avoids jury trials against contractors, and removing it could raise the cost and disrupt the operations of contractors performing weapons work for the government [S2][S3].

The deadline relief is limited: claims whose filing window would expire within a year of enactment get only a one-year grace period before being barred forever, so some very old claims would still be lost even under the bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a narrowly defined group of radiation victims, the bill offers something concrete: the right to sue the companies that actually ran the test sites, plus a second chance for people whose cases were dismissed. The cost is borne by the contractors facing liability and, indirectly, by the defense programs that rely on them. The bill is a targeted liability fix rather than a broad compensation program, so its overall public impact depends on how many viable claims still existed by 1989.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, where it sat without any hearing, markup, or floor vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Vucanovich (R-NV) introduced the bill on May 9, 1989, with Rep. Bilbray as an original cosponsor [S1][S3][S5].
It was referred jointly to the House Armed Services and Judiciary Committees the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 15, 1989, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Administrative Law and Governmental Relations, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 101st Congress [S5].
The bill drew only two cosponsors total — one Democrat and one Republican — and never reached the House floor [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private contractors that ran the nuclear weapons testing programs kept the 1985 liability shield, and radiation victims were left with the federal government as their only defendant.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from both Nevada representatives but only three supporters in total, and no recorded votes or floor debate show where the parties stood; it simply never moved in committee.

industries.industry: Private nuclear weapons testing and site-management contractors
industries.note: The bill would repeal the 1985 law that substituted the federal government as the defendant in radiation-injury suits and made the Tort Claims Act the sole remedy, exposing contractors to direct lawsuits and jury verdicts. Because the bill died, the contractors kept their shield, and victims could not reach them in court.

industries.industry: Federal government (Treasury and Justice, as defendant under the Tort Claims Act)
industries.note: Under the 1985 law the government stands in as defendant and pays judgments under the Tort Claims Act, which caps damages; the bill would shift that exposure back to contractors. Repeal could reduce government payouts while increasing contractor liability.
